summary: Describes a set of MIME types for use with the ISO Interlibrary Loan (ILL) protocol, which libraries use to request items from one another. The types let ILL messages be carried in MIME-based systems such as email. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Libraries lend books to each other and send request forms back and forth. This document gives those forms a proper label so email programs know what is inside the package.

subtitle: A standard way to send library loan request forms by email

tldr.problem: Libraries around the world need to request books from each other, but email systems do not know how to handle the special request forms the Interlibrary Loan protocol uses.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines two MIME types so email programs can recognize and handle ISO ILL protocol messages: one for the encoded requests themselves, and one for document delivery instructions.
tldr.outcome: Email systems can now properly carry library loan requests between institutions, allowing libraries to use email as a transport for their interlibrary loan workflow.

today: RFC 2503 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It defines a registration that allows ILL protocol messages to be carried in MIME-based systems.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.content:
The ISO Interlibrary Loan (ILL) protocol is a standard way for libraries to request materials from each other. Libraries use it to ask partners to find and send books or documents.

The ISO ILL protocol messages are encoded using Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1), with the Basic Encoding Rules (BER) as the encoding method. These are international standards for describing and encoding structured data in a language-neutral way. However, when these encoded messages travel through email systems, those systems need to know what kind of content is arriving. This is what MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) types do: they label the content so email programs understand how to handle it.

This RFC registers two MIME types to let email systems properly carry ILL protocol messages and the associated document delivery instructions.
sections.plainLanguage: Libraries send special request forms to each other through email. The email needs to know what kind of message is inside, so we give it a label that says 'this is a library loan request'.

sections.title: The Two MIME Types
sections.content:
The RFC defines two MIME types. The first is application/iso-10161-ill-1, which carries BER-encoded ISO ILL Protocol Data Units (PDUs). These are the actual interlibrary loan requests, answers, recalls and other transaction messages that libraries exchange.

The second is application/ill-ddi, which carries Document Delivery Instructions (DDI). DDI is an emerging protocol that allows a request management system to send delivery details to a delivery module and receive status reports back. It works together with the ILL protocol to automate the entire request and delivery process.
sections.plainLanguage: The first label is for the actual request message. The second label is for the delivery instructions that say when and how to send the book.

sections.title: Parameters and Encoding
sections.content:
Both MIME types include a required parameter called transfer-encoding. This parameter describes how the data has been prepared for email transport. The currently registered value is iso-8825-ber, which indicates the content is BER-encoded according to ISO standard 8825.

Since BER-encoded data is binary, it cannot be sent directly through 7-bit or 8-bit email systems without additional encoding. The RFC recommends using Base64 encoding to wrap the BER data into text that email systems can safely carry. Base64 converts binary data into a safe ASCII representation.

An optional parameter, iso-10161-apdu-type, can specify the type of the message (such as ILL-Request, ILL-Answer, Recall, or Shipped). While the actual type is always encoded in the data itself, this parameter helps for informational and diagnostic purposes.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIME type includes a note saying 'this is BER-encoded binary data'. The actual data is wrapped in Base64 so email can carry it. An optional note can say what kind of message it is.

sections.title: Message Types and Usage
sections.content:
The ILL protocol defines many message types to handle different aspects of the loan process. These include ILL-Request (asking to borrow an item), Forward-Notification (passing a request onward), Shipped (the item is on the way), ILL-Answer (answering a request), Conditional-Reply (cannot fulfill without changes), Cancel (ending a request), Received (item arrived at requestor), Recalled (item must be returned), and several status and notification messages.

In a single MIME message, each body part carries at most one BER-encoded PDU or DDI. However, a message containing multiple MIME body parts can transport multiple requests or responses in one email transmission, making it efficient for bulk transfers.
sections.plainLanguage: There are different types of messages for different stages: 'I want to borrow a book', 'I found one', 'I sent it', 'I got it', and so on. Each email can carry one or more messages.

sections.title: Interoperability and Standards
sections.content:
BER is an international standard for encoding structured data designed for systems that may store data differently internally. Using a standard encoding like BER makes it possible for library systems from different vendors and countries to exchange loan requests reliably.

The RFC anticipates that other encoding schemes might be used in the future, such as EDIFACT (which ISO 10161 also describes). By making the transfer-encoding parameter explicit, the MIME types are extensible: new encoding methods can be added without breaking existing deployments.

The National Library of Canada has been designated as the maintenance agency for the ISO ILL protocol. This official stewardship ensures the protocol continues to evolve in coordination with the ISO standardization process.
sections.plainLanguage: Using standard ways to code the messages lets computers from different countries talk to each other. The system is designed so new coding methods can be added later if needed.
